New Yorkers often pride themselves on their navigation expertise: whether it is finding a commute with the fewest subway transfers or the best way to secure a reservation in a packed restaurant. But when it comes to exploring the world outside of the five boroughs and checking off bucket list trips, this isn’t always the case. Questions like, “How do I pack for hiking at the Grand Canyon?” and “where am I going to find space to store all this gear?” start to creep in. If you've ever wondered how to make an outdoorsy adventure more feasible, keep reading.
For Nicole Goulet, a New York City trauma surgeon and surgical intensivist, spending so much time in the hospital caring for COVID patients led her to seek quiet moments outside of the city. In 2021, Nicole signed up for a four-day, three-night backpacking trip to Death Valley with Wildland Trekking, an Intrepid Company. She arrived with the understandable nerves of a first-time backpacker and left with something she hadn't known she needed: the freedom of being disconnected.
“I loved it so much that when we were walking out of the park that final day, I got sad to have to turn my phone back on again,” Nicole recalls. “At that time, I always needed to have my phone on because of work, so it was an amazing feeling to just not even have the option to have my phone on as there was no service for four days.” (Note: all Wildland guides carry emergency communication devices, which include a satellite phone and/or a GPS locator/texting device.)
On this trip, Death Valley delivered a surprise: four inches of snow in the middle of a Californian desert that is famous for being one of the hottest and driest places in North America (via NPS).
Another high point (pun intended) from her Death Valley trip was reaching the peak of their hike after traversing the mountains and rock formations. “It was so quiet, peaceful and stunning. It was an amazing feeling since in NYC and the hospitals, I am constantly surrounded by people. This and the beautiful sky full of stars are things we do not get to experience in the city.”
Exploring an International Dark Sky Park like Death Valley National Park offers a striking contrast to the bright lights and bustling energy of everyday life in the city, giving guests the opportunity to reconnect with the stillness of the natural world.
Since her first trip, Nicole has been on many trips with Wildland to parks including Yellowstone in 2024 and Yosemite in 2023 and again in 2026. She now takes annual treks with her mother each year. “The trips with my mom are normally either portered or animal assisted because she cannot hike with a large heavy pack, but loves to hike and also camp in the middle of nowhere in a tent!”
Nicole spotlights the Wildland community as a highlight of her trips throughout the years. “You get to meet a great group of very interesting people no matter what trip you take. You also get to know amazing trip leaders. I met Liz Lucas on my very first Wildland trip to Death Valley, we remained in contact and then I got to catch up with her again on this last trip to Yosemite. Liz is such an amazing guide, and I was so inspired by her on that first trip.”
Liz’s own path into the outdoors began with the California Conservation Corps Backcountry Trails program, where she found a love for guiding and public land stewardship. Her journey then took her to New Zealand where she further immersed herself in the outdoor industry, and she has now worked with Wildland as a guide for over five years.
She describes the rewarding experiences that come with being a Wildland guide, saying “I find that when I am out on the trail with guests, I get the honor of witnessing them regulating their nervous systems. I see a childlike awe of the world around us, and an increase in self-awareness and capability that they didn't know they had.”
Liz says that Wildland guides are there for guests every step of the journey, no matter their experience or skill level. “While there can be concern about having the right gear, we provide a robust packing list and advise on what is necessary for the trip. A guide will take on all logistics and will give you a plethora of information ranging from natural interpretation to human history.”
In terms of multi-day gear, Wildland provides nearly all of the necessities, including backpacks, trekking poles, tents, sleeping pads, sleeping bags, cooking gear, eating utensils and more. (Check out their website for additional gear-related details.)
For day hiking, according to Liz, the essentials are straightforward: “Good footwear, good snacks, enough water and a good attitude will put you in the top tier of new hikers in National Parks.” All things that can easily fit in city dwelling of any size!
Ready to trade the city hustle and bustle for a sky full of stars? Wildland Trekking offers backpacking trips, horse/llama/porter supported hikes, inn-based hiking tours, basecamp hiking tours and day hike tours in National Parks and Wilderness Areas worldwide. F and G trains have ground to a near halt the MTA said Friday evening, resulting in delays throughout the transit system.
Signal issues were once again the culprit according to city and state officials, this time during the Friday night rush. Passengers were spilling out onto the streets at stations along the two lines in Brooklyn.
At 7:30 p.m. the MTA reported there was no F service between ‌Brooklyn and Manhattan and no G service between Church Avenue and Bedford-Nostrand Avenues.
The stoppage followed delays on the 4 and 5 trains earlier in the day after officials said a passenger was struck.
The subway delays also came as the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights across the nation amid a communications meltdown at the federal level.

Even as planes start flying again, travelers using New York City and New Jersey airports are likely to face some excruciating delays.
The Federal Aviation Administration at 8:15 p.m. lifted a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports after an hourslong delay. The agency had halted all flights Friday afternoon, citing a "temporary telecommunications outage."
The FAA experienced "instability" with the Terminal Radar Approach Control across the country at around 3:30 p.m., according to U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy who spoke at a Friday evening press briefing. TRACON is an air traffic control facility that guides planes through the airspace around airports during departures and arrivals.
The system uses analog telecom parts, and the switches and routers got overloaded with data, resulting in intermittent communication and radar, Duffy said.
The FAA decided to halt all flights out of an abundance of caution, with over 3,500 planes in the air, he said.
U.S. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was nothing to indicate that the system was affected by a cyber attack or connected to the Microsoft outage, and the issue was "mechanically driven."
"There's no chatter," Mullin said at the briefing. "We haven't seen any footprints, as you would say, or identifications of people that got into the system."
As air traffic reopens, New York’s three airports will have longer delays than elsewhere in the country because of the large number of flights and limited number of runways and flight paths, according to Vikrant Vaze, a professor of engineering at Dartmouth College who studies transportation systems.
“New York airspace is very complicated because there are three large, very busy airports very close to each other,” he told Gothamist. “There is a huge amount of demand and New York is also spatially restricted so you cannot have massive airports anywhere nearby."
The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey referred all questions to the FAA, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
This is the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023 when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned, according to the Associated Press. Before that, the last time had been after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
The FAA grounded all flights due to a temporary telecommunications outage on Nov. 13, 2026. Passengers wait at Terminal 5 at John F. Kennedy Airport for more information.
Courtesy of Thomas Repe
John F. Kennedy Airport, LaGuardia Airport and Newark Liberty International Airport all advised travelers to confirm their flight status with their airline before heading to the airport. But even when systems are back up, local travelers should temper their hopes.
Vaze compared the ground stop in New York to a clogged pipe with a growing reservoir of water trying to get through. Because New York’s pipe is so narrow, unclogging it means the backup water will take a long time to get through.
“There is a very narrow window between how many aircraft can take off or land per hour at New York airports,” he said.
There were over 7,500 flights that were cancelled by 9:30 p.m., and over 25,000 delays nationwide, according to FlightAware.
The ground stop came just as Thomas Repe’s flight to Sarasota, Florida left the gate at Terminal 5 at JFK.
“We waited about 15 minutes and then they said, ‘Yep you got to get off,’” said Repe, adding that he’s not optimistic he’ll make it to Florida.
Passengers wait for information at JFK Airport after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a ground stop for all U.S. airports on Nov. 13, 2026.
Courtesy of Thomas Repe
Jason Haber was also traveling from JFK to Fort Lauderdale when flights were grounded.
“Initially the airport looked just as it would on any other day,” he said as he waited for this flight in Terminal 4. “Then all of a sudden you started to see as word got around the help desk line getting very long and people sitting down and lines forming.”
Haber ended up canceling his flight and plans to rebook in the coming days.
This is a developing story and was updated with new information.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has declined to endorse Brooklyn native U.S. Sen. Chuck Schumer as the next Senate majority leader, a signal that New York’s senior senator is facing increased pushback within the ranks of the Democratic party, including in the Empire State.
Mamdani was asked during a news conference on Friday if Schumer, who currently leads the Senate minority, deserved another term as leader when Democrats take majority control of the chamber in January. Instead of responding directly, the mayor said the American people voted for change in the midterm elections.
“They sent a message that they want Democratic leadership across the board that will deliver material improvements for the working class. And as the mayor of New York City, that's exactly what I want to see for New Yorkers across our five boroughs,” Mamdani said. “So I care less about who it is, and I care more about what they do with that power.”
Mamdani’s decision not to back Schumer is reminiscent of the senator’s own refusal to endorse Mamdani last year after Mamdani won the Democratic nomination for mayor. Even on the day of the mayoral election, Schumer would not tell reporters who he voted for and would only say he looked forward to “working with the next mayor.”
Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders have all said they would not support Schumer as their party leader.
Schumer led the Senate in 2021 and 2022, when Democrats held a slim majority with then-Vice President Kamala Harris serving as the tiebreaking vote. During that period, Congress passed several major pieces of legislation including the COVID-19 stimulus package and the bipartisan infrastructure law, which earmarked billions of dollars in aid to New York.
Late Thursday, Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen officially announced he planned to challenge Schumer for Majority Leader. In a statement posted to social media, Van Hollen said the American people demanded new leadership.
“In this election, Americans called on us to unrig an economy rigged against working people & fueled by political corruption. To deliver, we need new leadership,” Van Hollen wrote on X. “This isn't about any one person — it’s about answering that call. That's why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”
On Friday, the Working Families Party said that it was supporting Van Hollen for the Senate leadership post.
Schumer responded to Van Hollen’s announcement on Thursday night.
“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader,” Schumer wrote on X. “I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.”
A spokesperson for Schumer referred to his existing statement when asked for a response to Mamdani’s comments.
Senate leadership elections are scheduled to take place in December.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced his pick for the so-called nightlife mayor Friday: a freelance web developer who recently served as cochair of New York City’s chapter of the Democratic Socialist of America.
Eric Thor’s appointment to lead the Office of Nightlife was announced in a Paper Magazine profile portraying him as a familiar figure in the city’s lefty political scene and a regular clubgoer in East Williamsburg and Bushwick.
The role has gained increasing prominence as other cities establish similar offices focused on nightlife. But Thor’s hiring came as a surprise to Andrew Rigie, the executive director of the influential New York City Hospitality Alliance.
Rigie serves as the chair of advisory board for the Office of Nightlife, which was established to work with the director and administration on nightlife matters.
“It’s strikingly bizarre that they wouldn’t reach out to the Office of Nightlife Advisory Board,” he said.
Rigie said the job of nightlife mayor serves as both an ambassador for the city’s diverse hospitality scene and government liaison who can help establishments cut red tape and mediate disputes with residents.
Following a boost from the Knicks historic playoff run and World Cup, many establishments say they are struggling. A recent survey of 275 bars and restaurants by Rigie’s hospitality alliance found that owners were either breaking even or operating at a loss during the third quarter of this year.
Thor, an Astoria resident who works as a freelance web developer, worked on both Mamdani’s state assembly and mayoral campaigns. His LinkedIn profile states that he “guided the mayoral endorsement process of Zohran K. Mamdani” for the NYC-DSA. His website cites a digital affordability calculator he created for his campaign that shows how much New Yorkers might save under Mamdani.
His online resume does not include any experience working in the nightlife industry.
In a press release, Mamdani described the city’s nightlife as a “lifeline for small businesses” and praised Thor’s experience as a political organizer.
“Eric has spent years organizing alongside working people and he will bring that same commitment building a nightlife economy that works for everyone,” Mamdani said.
Ariel Palitz, the city’s first nightlife mayor, said Thor reached out to her on Friday.
“Although it’s not yet clear to me what his nightlife experience is, I’m sure he and I will be having many conversations,” said Palitz, who now runs a consulting group on nightlife policy.
“I’m just grateful that the mayor sees the value in this office,” she added.
Thor referred questions to the mayor’s press office. The mayor’s office did not respond to Gothamist’s inquiry about the appointment process and Thor’s salary.
Jeffrey Garcia, the previous nightlife director appointed by then-Mayor Eric Adams, earned $146,000, according to data compiled by the Empire Center.
Garcia, who declined to comment, was a former NYPD detective. He previously owned a coffee and wine bar in the Bronx.

New York City activated its first Code Blue of the season on Friday, opening warming centers overnight and relaxing shelter intake rules as temperatures and wind chills are expected to approach freezing, officials said.
The cold weather emergency runs from 4 p.m. Friday to 8 a.m. Saturday, according to the city Department of Emergency Management. Temperatures in Central Park are expected to fall to about 36 degrees, with windchills as low as 34, but colder air moving in after a storm could push both closer to freezing, the agency said, citing the National Weather Service.
It’s the first Code Blue since Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced an expanded plan this week, after more than two dozen people died outdoors or in their homes during a stretch of freezing weather last winter. The city promised $25 million in new funding, 300 more outreach canvassers, 800 more beds and 20 warming buses for the season, aimed to help New Yorkers sleeping on the street.
But last winter showed the danger isn’t limited to people living outside. Gothamist found that at least five of the people who died outside during the cold stretch that began in January had housing.
On Friday, six warming buses are scheduled to run overnight, from midnight to 5 a.m. Saturday at Bellevue, Elmhurst, Harlem and Lincoln hospitals and at Penn Station, according to city officials. Eight drop-in centers are open, and three of those hospitals are serving as warming centers from 4 p.m. to 8 a.m.
“When Code Blue is in effect, we make it as easy as possible for anyone to come inside,” Department of Social Services Commissioner Erin Dalton said in a statement.
Anyone who walks into a city shelter or drop-in center will be let in without the usual intake steps, she said.
NYC Emergency Management Commissioner Christina Farrell urged New Yorkers to check on older neighbors “and anyone who lives alone.”
She also warned that fire is the biggest risk of staying warm at home.
Officials are asking anyone who sees someone outside who may need help to call 311, and to call 911 if a person is in danger, seems confused or appears very cold. Warming locations are listed at on.nyc.gov/warm.

When Eric Ulrich asked then-Department of Correction Commissioner Louis Molina to consider hiring his friend’s daughter for an open position in February 2022, Molina said he set up a meeting that same week.
Ulrich, then a senior adviser to Mayor Eric Adams, called Molina to recommend the daughter of his friend Michael Mazzio, according to a recording played in court on Friday. By the end of Molina’s one-on-one “exploratory conversation” with the recent college graduate, Mazzio’s daughter had a conditional job offer for an entry-level analyst position.
“She had the job if she wanted it,” Molina testified in court Friday.
Prosecutors have since accused Mazzio of bribing Ulrich with premium season tickets to the New York Mets in exchange for favors, including helping to secure the job for his daughter. A trial is ongoing in Manhattan against both men, who have pleaded not guilty.
Phone calls played in Manhattan court on Friday reveal new details about how Ulrich convinced Molina to interview Mazzio’s daughter and followed up to ensure the hiring process was moving along.
“Mazzio’s the priority,” Ulrich said in a recorded phone call played in court on Friday.
“You got it,” Molina replied.
Ulrich was the first member of Adams’ inner circle to face corruption charges — but not the last. The former City Council member served as an aide to the mayor, and later as his commissioner of the Department of Buildings.
The Manhattan district attorney’s office has accused Ulrich of using his power in the administration to benefit friends and associates who were willing to compensate him with cash and other perks. Mazzio was one of those friends, according to prosecutors. The DA’s office said Ulrich tried to use his influence to help Mazzio resolve licensing issues with a towing company he owns, in addition to helping his daughter get a city job.
In court on Friday, Molina said he didn’t know Mazzio. But the former jails commissioner said he always personally interviewed candidates when he received a referral directly from a member of the mayor’s staff — something that he said happened “six to 12” times during his approximately two years leading the department.
“To be clear, would you have interviewed Kristina Mazzio, but for the referral of Mr. Ulrich?” Assistant District Attorney Guy Tardanico asked Molina in court.
“No,” he replied.
In phone calls played in court for the first time on Friday, Ulrich repeatedly complimented Molina.
During one phone call shortly after Molina’s appointment, Ulrich said “the mayor could not have picked a better person” and referred to the new commissioner as “Johnny-on-the-spot,” according to a recording played in court.
Molina faced criticism throughout his tenure as Department of Correction commissioner. While he was overseeing Rikers Island, a federal monitor found that conditions in the jail complex were deteriorating. His first year as commissioner, 2022, was the deadliest year for New York City jails in a quarter of a century.
In an April 2022 call, Ulrich asked Molina about his recent experience being interviewed in the media. He encouraged the commissioner to tell his “own story” about the job he was doing.
“You can’t let them tell the story for you,” Ulrich said, according to a recording presented as evidence in court.
“Exactly,” Molina replied. “And then we’ve got these constant hit pieces.”
Molina testified that, although he did hire Kristina Mazzio daughter, he did not hire her as director of special projects — the position Ulrich initially recommended her for. The person in that role would be responsible for coordinating visits to Rikers Island for advocates and elected officials, and Molina said Mazzio’s daughter was not qualified.
Instead, he suggested that Kristina Mazzio consider a food service job or a policy analyst position. He testified that he suggested those roles after learning that she was interested in baking pastries and also seemed to have “solid administrative skills.”
“She told me she was interested in the policy analyst position,” Molina testified.
The former commissioner said he wasn’t aware of anyone else being interviewed for the job, which paid $50,000. After human resources vetted her, she was hired.

The city education department will review its hiring practices after learning that the man accused of killing a Brooklyn jogger last month was previously hired as a paraprofessional, despite a documented history of mental health concerns.
Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels announced Friday that the city’s Law Department will conduct the independent review and deliver recommendations.
“The safety of our students and staff is our highest priority. We can leave no stone unturned and no path unexplored when it comes to protecting that safety,” Samuels said in a statement.
Sayed Mohassib, 27, is accused of fatally stabbing Katie Suarez as she jogged on the Shore Parkway Greenway on Oct. 30. Mohassib worked as a paraprofessional at PS 200, which is only blocks from the greenway that passes under the Verrazzano Bridge. He has pleaded not guilty.
According to city records, Mohassib was first hired by the education department in 2019. He then left the school system and graduated from the NYPD’s police academy in 2022. He only worked for the NYPD for a month before being granted military leave to join the U.S. Marines. He was then discharged from the Marines due to psychiatric issues. He tried to rejoin the NYPD in 2023, but NYPD supervisors were so concerned by his behavior he was taken to Bellevue Hospital, officials said.
Nevertheless, Mohassib was rehired as a paraprofessional in 2024, payroll records show.
Parents and local officials have demanded to know why Mohassib was allowed to work closely with public school children after the NYPD, where he had also worked briefly as a police officer, raised serious concerns about his mental stability.
The majority of the city’s paraprofessionals work closely with students with disabilities who have individualized education programs, commonly known as IEPs.
New York City Council member Kayla Santosuosso had earlier this week called for a review of the education department’s personnel policies in light of the murder.
“I’m looking at what happened that led up to this person continuing to be employed by the DOE and in such an intimate way with students,” she said. “My concern is that there seem to be numerous red flags along the way that some system within the DOE should have caught.”
Santosuosso said school staff who had worked with Mohassib in the past had also reached out to her office this week to say they had raised concerns about his behavior. The education department did not respond to requests for comments about why he continued to be employed despite those concerns, or after the NYPD had rejected him.
The city has been struggling with a shortage of paraprofessionals for years. The United Federation of Teachers is suing the city over legislation to raise pay for paraprofessionals in order to recruit and retain more candidates.
According to the criminal complaint, Mohassib denied killing Suarez but told investigators that he was sitting on a bench along the path and became “covered in blood.”
Surveillance footage of Mohassib running from the scene of the murder, entering his apartment building and then walking out about 15 minutes later to throw items in the garbage, according to a complaint.
Jessica Battaglia, a former teacher at the High School of Telecommunication Arts and Technology, who said she knew Mohassib when he was in ninth grade, said it was shocking to learn that the “sweet” kid she taught could be arrested for murder.
She said Mohassib stood out for his kindness to classmates, especially students with disabilities. “He was one of our favorite students, that’s why we’re so shocked,” she said. She remembered him winning awards that year at an end-of-year ceremony, and said the person she knew more than a decade ago would have been a “perfect” candidate for a job working with children with disabilities.
She noted the news reports that indicated someone missed multiple signs of his deteriorating mental health. “Why didn’t anyone help him before he hurt someone else?” she asked.
